newsitem.title: USA: Boeing lays out structure of merged company.
newsitem.headline: Boeing lays out structure of merged company.

text.p: Boeing Co. Monday unveiled a new corporate structure reflecting vastly expanded military and space operations after its $16.3 billion acquisition of former rival McDonnell Douglas Corp.

Boeing Chairman Phil Condit and President Harry Stonecipher announced the post-merger organization at a Washington news conference beamed by satellite to rallies attended by most of the manufacturer's 220,000 employees.

"This is Boeing time," declared Condit, noting that the Seattle-based company is now the world's largest aerospace company, with expected sales this year of $49 billion and an order backlog of more than $100 billion.
Under the new organization, Alan Mulally, who was appointed this year to run Boeing's defense and space group, will be president of an enlarged information, space and defense systems group.

The group will include a military aircraft and business unit, based in St. Louis, a space systems division in Seal Beach, Calif., and a Seattle-based unit focusing on satellites, strategic missiles and other systems.

Shortly after the merger became effective Friday, Boeing named a veteran executive to run its former Douglas Aircraft unit, which will be part of Boeing's commercial airplane group, based in the Seattle area.

Boeing also said it had formed an eight-member executive council, including two former McDonnell Douglas executives, reporting to Condit and Stonecipher, who had been president and chief executive officer of McDonnell Douglas.
Wolfgang Demisch, an analyst at BT Securities, said he thought the new corporate structure reflected "an effort to try to achieve some clear evidence that this was a merger rather than a takeover."
Condit said the changes announced so far were the start of a transition he hoped to have mostly completed by year-end.
He said he expected "some" layoffs, mainly in back office areas where functions were duplicated, but did not elaborate.
But he said that even employees affected by consolidation probably would be able to find work within the company because business was growing so rapidly.

While many analysts have said McDonnell Douglas commercial jets that competed with Boeing models did not have a future, Condit said he did not mind the overlap as long as orders go to Boeing and not its European rival Airbus Industrie.
And Stonecipher said the acquisition by Boeing may improve prospects for the the MD-80/90, MD-95 and MD-11 jets, which have won few orders in recent years.
"I happen to be of the opinion that now that we are one company and have the strength of Boeing, that those products will sell better," Stonecipher said.
He pointed in particular to the new twin-engine MD-95, which has not won any orders since the product was launched in 1995 with a sale of 50 planes to ValuJet Inc.

"One of the questions was always, 'Is Douglas going to be around? Are you committed to the business?" Stonecipher said. "I think clearly people don't have to ask that question anymore, and when you have those products in a Boeing salesman's bag -- the new Boeing -- it has a better opportunity."
The company also unveiled a new logo -- a stylized jet and ringed globe inspired by the old McDonnell Douglas symbol.
